passage:
"Mummy, is it cheating if I check my subtraction with adding?"
Shalini looked up from her laptop. "Show me."
Pankaj pointed. "Forty-three minus eighteen is twenty-five. So twenty-five plus eighteen should go back to forty-three."
"Does it?"
He scribbled. "Twenty-five plus eighteen... forty-three! It goes back!"
"That's not cheating. That's checking."
"It's like the ice cubes. They melt, then you freeze them again, and it's ice again."
"Is everything like that?"
He thought. "Not the roti. You can't un-cook it."
Shalini laughed. "Good catch."

qa.q: Which subtraction did Pankaj check?
qa.a: Forty-three minus eighteen is twenty-five.

qa.q: Why was Pankaj worried it might be cheating?
qa.a: He wasn't sure using addition to check was allowed, perhaps thinking each sum had to be done only one way.

qa.q: What could Shalini ask next to stretch his idea?
qa.a: She might ask him to find other operations that undo each other, like multiplying and dividing.

qa.q: How might Pankaj's teacher see him checking this way?
qa.a: As a sign that he understands how the operations link, not as cheating.

grounding: It shows a boy discovering that addition undoes subtraction and noticing which everyday changes can or cannot be reversed.

passage: Last month my friend Imran and I got lost in the old market. We'd turned left at the bangle shop, right at the temple, then left at the fruit stalls. Imran was panicking. I said, "Just do it backwards." So: right at the fruit stalls, left at the temple, right at the bangle shop. And there was the bus stop! Imran said, "Suraj, you're a genius!" I'm not. It's like undoing plus with minus in maths. You go back through the same steps, only reversed. I still think about how simple it felt once I saw it that way.

qa.q: What was the first turn the two friends took?
qa.a: They turned left at the bangle shop.

qa.q: Why did Suraj say "I'm not" when Imran called Suraj a genius?
qa.a: Suraj felt the idea was simple once seen as undoing the steps, like minus undoes plus.

qa.q: What could Imran do the next time Imran feels panicky when lost?
qa.a: Stop, remember the last few turns and retrace them in reverse, or ask a shopkeeper for directions.

qa.q: How did Imran see Suraj's idea?
qa.a: Imran was impressed and relieved, calling Suraj a genius after all that panicking.

grounding: It shows a child reversing a sequence of turns to return to the start, linking it to undoing operations in maths.

passage: Tuition note by Aditi, after Jatin's session. Jatin, ten, made a secret code today: each letter moves three places forward, so CAT became FDW. His friend couldn't read it. I asked, "How would he get the word back?" Jatin thought, then said, "Move each letter three places back." He decoded FDW to CAT on the board, then tried KHOOR himself and laughed when it became HELLO. He said, "It's like the minus that undoes plus." Next time I will give him a two-step code, so he has to reverse both steps in the right order.

qa.q: What did CAT become in Jatin's code?
qa.a: CAT became FDW.

qa.q: Why might Jatin have laughed when KHOOR became HELLO?
qa.a: He seemed delighted that undoing the steps actually worked and gave back a real word.

qa.q: Why is Aditi's two-step code a good next challenge?
qa.a: Jatin will have to undo both steps in reverse order, which deepens his grasp of reversing operations.

qa.q: What would change for his friend if he learned the rule too?
qa.a: He could decode Jatin's messages himself, turning the code into a shared game. 😊

grounding: It shows a child realising that shifting letters forward can be undone by shifting them back.

passage:
Tuesday
Dear Diary,
Today in maths I had 45 + 28 = 73. Ma'am said check it. I didn't know how. Then I thought: if I take the 28 back out of 73, I should get 45 again. 73 - 28... 45! It worked!! 🎉 At home I showed Mummy (Shalini) and she tested me with 60 - 25. I did 35 + 25 and got 60, so I knew it was right. It's like walking back the same road home. I tried it on 5 sums. All correct. I think I'll check everything this way now.
- Vandana

qa.q: What sum did Vandana check in maths class?
qa.a: In maths, Vandana had 45 + 28 = 73, and Ma'am said check it.

qa.q: How did Vandana feel when the check worked, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Vandana felt excited and proud, shown by the double exclamation marks and the party emoji.

qa.q: How could Vandana's teacher build on Vandana's discovery?
qa.a: The teacher could ask Vandana to explain the 'walking back' idea to the class and try it with multiplication and division.

qa.q: How might Shalini feel seeing Vandana check sums this way?
qa.a: She would likely feel pleased that Vandana understands why the method works, not just how to do it.

grounding: Illustrates a child realising that mathematical operations can be reversed to get back to the start, in a diary.

passage: In a small Goan village, Francis watched his uncle Hemant melt a lump of ghee in a pan for the Sunday cake. 'It's gone, it's water now,' Francis said. 'Is it?' said Hemant. He poured some into a steel bowl and put it on the window ledge in the breeze. By evening, Francis poked it. Solid again. His eyes widened. 'It came back!' Then he thought. 'So if I melt it again, it'll be liquid, and cool again, it'll be solid. Back and forth.' Hemant smiled and tied a knot in a string. 'Can you undo this?'

qa.q: Where did Hemant put the bowl of melted ghee?
qa.a: He put it on the window ledge in the breeze.

qa.q: What does Francis's widened eyes suggest he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he was surprised and excited to see the ghee return to its solid form.

qa.q: Why was Hemant's knot a clever next step?
qa.a: It gave Francis another chance to see that some actions can be undone to return to the start.

qa.q: What would change if Hemant had simply told Francis that ghee sets again?
qa.a: Francis would have missed discovering it himself, and the idea might not have stuck as well.

grounding: Shows a child realising that some changes can be reversed back to their original state, in a village.

passage: On a rainy afternoon in Buenos Aires, Valentina, eight, was checking her maths homework at the kitchen table. Her friend Nour looked over. "How do you know 47 plus 26 is 73?" Valentina grinned. "Watch. If I take 26 away from 73, I should get back to 47." She wrote it out. "Forty-seven! See, it goes backwards." Nour tried it with her own sum and found a mistake. "Oh no, mine doesn't go back." Valentina helped her fix it.

qa.q: What was Valentina's sum?
qa.a: 47 plus 26 is 73.

qa.q: How might Valentina have felt when her subtraction gave back 47?
qa.a: She felt pleased and confident that her answer was right.

qa.q: What could Nour try next time she's unsure of a sum?
qa.a: Use Valentina's trick of doing it backwards to check her answer.

qa.q: How might Nour feel when her sum didn't go back?
qa.a: A little disappointed at first, but glad to have found and fixed the mistake.

grounding: Shows a child realising that addition can be reversed with subtraction to get back to the start.

passage: In the school science lab, Naveen, the teacher, gave each group an ice cube in a steel bowl. "What happens if we put it in the sun?" Devika, nine, said, "It melts." "And then?" She thought. "If we put the water in the freezer, it goes back to ice." "So is it gone for ever?" "No! It just changed. We can change it back." Later she folded a paper boat, unfolded it carefully, and showed the flat sheet. "Same idea," she said.

qa.q: What did each group get in a steel bowl?
qa.a: An ice cube.

qa.q: What does Devika saying "No! It just changed" suggest about her thinking?
qa.a: She felt excited and confident, realising that some changes can be undone.

qa.q: How could Naveen build on Devika's paper-boat idea?
qa.a: Ask the class to find other changes that can or can't be undone, like melting chocolate or burning paper.

qa.q: How might the other children see Devika's paper-boat example?
qa.a: They might find it helpful, since it shows the idea with something they can hold.

grounding: Shows a child realising that changes like melting and folding can be reversed.

passage: I'm Ojas, Kalyani's brother. Kalyani, eight, spent an hour building a block tower that she said was a lighthouse. Then Nani said we needed the blocks for my cousin, who was visiting. Kalyani took it apart in exactly the reverse order, top block first, and lined them up so she could build it again later. "I know how to get it back," she said. Last year she'd have kicked it down and cried. I'm not sure what she was thinking, but she looked calm.

qa.q: What did Kalyani say her block tower was?
qa.a: A lighthouse.

qa.q: What might Kalyani have felt as she took the tower apart?
qa.a: She seemed calm, perhaps reassured that she could rebuild it by reversing her steps.

qa.q: How could Nani show she noticed Kalyani's careful approach?
qa.a: Thank her and later give her time to rebuild the lighthouse from her line of blocks.

qa.q: How does Ojas see Kalyani's change since last year?
qa.a: He is surprised she stayed calm instead of kicking it down and crying.

grounding: Shows a child understanding that a construction can be reversed and rebuilt, seen by her brother.

passage:
Monday: Devika wrote 9 + 4 = 13 in her notebook. Then Tanvir Bhaiya asked, "So what's 13 minus 4?" She started counting on her fingers from zero, frowning.
Thursday: Tanvir set out nine buttons, added four, then took the four away. "Back to nine," Devika said slowly. "Oh! Minus undoes plus."
Next Monday: Devika checked her own homework. For 25 + 8 = 33, she wrote 33 − 8 underneath and got 25. "It goes back, so it's right," she said, and ticked it, grinning.

qa.q: How many buttons did Tanvir set out first?
qa.a: Nine buttons.

qa.q: How did Devika feel when she said "Oh! Minus undoes plus"?
qa.a: She felt surprised and excited to discover that subtraction reverses addition.

qa.q: How could Tanvir build on what Devika learned?
qa.a: He could show her that division undoes multiplication, using buttons in the same way.

qa.q: How might Tanvir feel seeing Devika check her own homework?
qa.a: He would likely feel proud and pleased that his button lesson helped her.

grounding: Over a week, a girl learns that subtraction undoes addition and uses it to check sums.

passage: Urmila Nani put down her glasses. "Afreen, when I was nine, my father's old clock stopped. I took it apart on the floor, every screw and wheel, to see what was wrong. Then I panicked. I couldn't remember how it went back! My mother was coming home soon. So I sat still and thought: the last thing I took out goes in first. I laid the pieces in a line, backwards, and put them in one by one. When the clock ticked again, I nearly cried with relief. From then on, whenever I took anything apart, I laid the pieces in a row." Afreen looked at the clock on the wall. "That one?" "That one."

qa.q: What did young Urmila take apart?
qa.a: Her father's old clock.

qa.q: How did young Urmila feel when the clock ticked again?
qa.a: She felt huge relief, nearly crying.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and what habit did it lead to?
qa.a: Realising the last piece out must go in first; afterwards she always laid pieces in a row when taking things apart.

qa.q: How might Urmila's mother have reacted if she had come home to the clock in pieces?
qa.a: She might have been upset or worried about the clock, which is why young Urmila panicked.

grounding: A grandmother tells how, as a child, she rebuilt a clock by reversing the order she took it apart.

passage: It started pouring as Aditi and her little brother Naveen came out of the tuition centre, and the auto they usually took was gone. "Walk home," Aditi decided, though she had only done it once with Papa. She remembered the way there: left at the temple, right at the bakery, left at the post office. Naveen was shivering. "Which way?" Aditi thought hard. "Going back, we do it backwards. Right at the post office, left at the bakery, right at the temple." They splashed along, and there was their gate. Naveen squeezed her hand. "You're a genius." Aditi laughed, dripping.

qa.q: Where did they turn left on the way to the centre?
qa.a: At the temple and at the post office.

qa.q: How did Aditi feel when she had to find the way home in the rain?
qa.a: She felt nervous and under pressure, but determined as she worked it out.

qa.q: What worked in how Aditi planned the route home?
qa.a: She reversed the order of the turns and swapped each left for a right.

qa.q: How might Naveen have felt during the walk?
qa.a: He was probably cold and a bit scared, then relieved and proud of his sister when they reached home.

grounding: In the rain, a girl finds the way home by reversing a remembered route.

passage:
In the colony library in Kolkata, Jahnavi, eight, was stuck on her maths homework.

"Twelve plus seven is nineteen," she said to her brother Yash. "But what's nineteen minus seven?"

Yash, eleven, smiled. "Think. You added seven to get nineteen. What if you take it away again?"

Jahnavi frowned. Then her face lit up. "Twelve! Because it goes back!"

"Exactly."

She tried another. "Five plus eight is thirteen. So thirteen minus eight is five!"

She wrote three more pairs, grinning. "It's like walking forward and then walking back."

qa.q: What is twelve plus seven?
qa.a: Twelve plus seven is nineteen.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi feel when she understood?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt excited and proud, her face lighting up and grinning.

qa.q: How did Yash help Jahnavi understand reversibility?
qa.a: He asked her to think about taking the seven away again instead of giving the answer.

qa.q: How might Yash feel when Jahnavi worked it out?
qa.a: Yash was likely pleased and proud to see her understand.

grounding: A child realises that subtraction can undo addition, returning to the original number.

passage:
"Look, Damini," Amandeep said at the Lohri bonfire. He held up an ice cube from his glass.

"It'll melt."

"And then?"

"Water."

"Can it become ice again?"

Damini thought. "If you put it in the freezer."

"And the ghee we melted for the pinni?"

"It went hard again when it cooled."

"But the wood in the fire?"

Damini looked at the flames. "No. That's ash now. You can't make it wood again."

Amandeep grinned. "So some things go back, and some don't."

qa.q: What did Amandeep hold up?
qa.a: He held up an ice cube from his glass.

qa.q: How did Damini feel working out which changes go back?
qa.a: Damini felt thoughtful and interested, carefully reasoning about each change.

qa.q: How did Amandeep help Damini understand reversibility?
qa.a: He asked questions about ice, ghee and wood so she could reason out which changes reverse.

qa.q: How might Amandeep feel about Damini's answers?
qa.a: Amandeep seemed pleased, grinning at her reasoning.

grounding: At a Lohri bonfire, a child reasons about which changes can be reversed and which cannot.

passage:
The summer I was nine, my sister Vidya and I walked to the new library by ourselves for the first time. Left at the temple, right at the chai stall, straight past the park.

On the way back, I panicked. Everything looked different.

Vidya said, "Just do it backwards."

So I thought: we went straight past the park, so now go back past it. We turned right at the chai stall, so now turn left. We turned left at the temple, so now turn right.

We reached home. I'm Ramesh, and ever since, when I'm lost, I undo my steps one by one.

qa.q: Where did Ramesh and Vidya turn right on the way there?
qa.a: They turned right at the chai stall.

qa.q: How did Ramesh feel on the way back?
qa.a: Ramesh felt panicked and lost because everything looked different.

qa.q: How did Vidya help Ramesh find the way home?
qa.a: Vidya said to do the route backwards, reversing each turn.

qa.q: How might Vidya feel when they reached home?
qa.a: Vidya was probably relieved and proud that her idea worked.

grounding: A child remembers learning to reverse a route step by step to get home.

passage:
Tutor's note, Shimla, 20 January
It was so cold this week that a bowl of water on the school steps froze overnight. Nitin brought it in and watched it melt by the heater. "It can go back to ice if we put it out tonight," he said. Later we did sums. He wrote 8 + 6 = 14, and I asked what 14 − 6 would be. He stared, then grinned. "Eight! You just undo it, like the ice." He tried three more on his own. His friend Aman said, "That's a trick!" Nitin explained it to him. I've asked his mother to try "undo" questions at home.
Sangeeta Ma'am

qa.q: What sum did Nitin write?
qa.a: He wrote 8 + 6 = 14.

qa.q: What does Nitin's grin after answering "Eight!" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt excited and proud at discovering that a sum can be undone, just like the ice.

qa.q: What else could Nitin's mother ask to build on this?
qa.a: She could ask "undo" questions like "If I add 3 and then take away 3, where are we?", or let him fold and unfold paper.

qa.q: How does Aman react to Nitin's discovery?
qa.a: Aman thinks it's a trick at first, then gets to hear Nitin explain it.

grounding: Illustrates a child realising that melting ice and an addition sum can both be reversed back to where they started.
